theme: Fear God; wealth’s emptiness; wisdom’s limits
readingInstruction: Read Ecclesiastes 5:1-7:29. These chapters include advice on worship, the problem of wealth, and reflections on wisdom and death. Notice the practical tone.
settingTheScene: The Preacher shifts from observation to counsel. After describing the futility of life under the sun, he offers advice on how to live well within it. He speaks of approaching God, the limits of wealth, and the value of mourning. The tone is sober, and the advice is realistic. It is the voice of an experienced teacher.
observation: “Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. To draw near to listen is better than to offer the sacrifice of fools” (5:1).
“God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few” (5:2).
“He who loves money will not be satisfied with money, nor he who loves wealth with his income” (5:10).
“As he came from his mother’s womb he shall go again, naked as he came, and shall take nothing for his toil” (5:15).
“Every man also to whom God has given wealth and possessions and power to enjoy them, and to accept his lot and rejoice in his toil, this is the gift of God” (5:19).
“It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting, for this is the end of all mankind, and the living will lay it to heart” (7:2).
“In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider: God has made the one as well as the other” (7:14).
“Surely there is no one on earth who is righteous, who does good and never sins” (7:20).
interpretation:
The Preacher begins with worship. “Guard your steps when you go to the house of God.” He warns against thoughtless religion: hurried words, empty vows, and the “sacrifice of fools.” To listen is better than to offer. “God is in heaven and you are on earth. Therefore let your words be few.” It is the posture of reverence. We approach a holy God with humility and attention, not with a flood of words.

The long section on wealth makes several observations. Money does not satisfy: “He who loves money will not be satisfied.” The more one has, the more people there are to consume it. Wealth can be lost in a bad venture. And at death, one leaves with nothing. The Preacher has no patience for the idea that riches bring security. Yet he does not say wealth is evil. The gift is that God enables a person to enjoy what he has. “This is the gift of God.” The ability to enjoy is itself a gift.

Chapter 7 gathers a series of “better than” sayings that seem strange at first. Better to go to the house of mourning than to a feast. Better sorrow than laughter. Better the rebuke of a wise man than the song of fools. The reason is that grief teaches. A funeral reminds us of the end and makes us wise. Those who avoid thinking about death live carelessly.

The Preacher gives an honest comment on the limits of wisdom. He tried to be wise, but it was “far from me.” He admits that there is much he cannot understand. He also says that God has made both prosperity and adversity, and that we cannot predict the future. The wise do not demand to know everything.

The chapter ends with a sober statement of human sinfulness: “No one on earth is righteous, who does good and never sins.” And with a key diagnosis: “God made man upright, but they have sought out many schemes.” The problem is not creation but the Fall.
connection: Paul quotes Ecclesiastes 7:20 in the same spirit in Romans 3:10-12. Jesus warned against empty words in prayer (Matthew 6:7). 1 Timothy 6:6-10 says that godliness with contentment is great gain, and that the love of money is the root of all kinds of evils. Jesus said, “Blessed are those who mourn” (Matthew 5:4). He is the one who is without sin (Hebrews 4:15), the righteous one the Preacher could not find.
application:
Before your next time of worship or prayer, slow down. Listen before you speak.

Ask whether money is satisfying you or driving you. Practice contentment today.

Sit with mortality for a few minutes. What does it teach you about how to live?
prayerPrompts: Ask God to teach you to listen more than you speak.
Ask him to keep you from loving money.
Tell him where you want to be satisfied in him.
